title: One man for the people (John 11:45–57)
hookLine: the council plots; Caiaphas says it's better one man die

cards: A room, worried people, and someone saying the hard, practical thing out loud. After Lazarus walks out of the tomb, many who saw it believe.

Some go to Jerusalem and report what happened, and the chief priests and leaders call an emergency meeting of the council. Their question is frightened, and very human: "What do we? for this man doeth many miracles."
They're not debating whether the miracle happened. They're asking what it will cost them.

teach.b: First, the pressure on the room. Judea was under Roman occupation. Rome let the temple and its leaders keep a measure of authority, as long as there was order.
Crowds, excitement, talk of a king: that was exactly what Rome crushed.
The council says it plainly: "If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation." Their fear wasn't imaginary.
Decades later, Roman armies did destroy the temple.
Then the high priest that year, Caiaphas, speaks: "Ye know nothing at all, nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not."
Expedient means useful, the practical choice. One life traded for many: an old logic, sacrifice one to keep the peace. And then John does something remarkable.
He says Caiaphas spoke better than he knew.
Being high priest, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, "and not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad."
The same sentence, heard two ways. Caiaphas meant politics. John hears the gospel in it.
From that day, John says, they made plans.

teach.h: ONE MAN SHOULD DIE FOR THE PEOPLE.
teach.b: Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness. Passover is near, and the whole city wonders: will he come to the feast? It was Rome that would carry out the execution.
But the road toward it begins in a frightened room.

how: Many churches pray for those in authority in their regular services; Christians read Caiaphas's words as an unknowing prophecy that Jesus would die for many.

o: a council member who spoke up to defend Jesus
the Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to the cross
the high priest who said one man should die for the people

games.q: what's inside John 11:45–57 — tap the pairs.

s: the council doubted that Lazarus had really been raised
they said, "this man doeth many miracles." their worry was the cost.
the council feared Rome would take away their place and nation
and decades later, Roman armies did destroy the temple.
John says Caiaphas's words held a meaning he didn't intend
he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather the scattered.

games.q: you're on the council. crowds are following a miracle worker, and Rome is watching. what does Caiaphas propose?
o: invite him to address the council.
let one man die so the whole nation doesn't perish.
do nothing and see what happens.
games.why: "it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people." John hears in it more than Caiaphas meant.

practice: Think of someone who makes hard decisions for others, a mayor, a head of state, a school principal, a hospital director, a manager at work, and imagine the weight of their room: competing fears, real dangers, people who'll be hurt either way.
You don't have to agree with them; just picture them as people under pressure.
If you pray, pray for them by name, for wisdom and courage, and that no one is sacrificed for convenience; if not, hold them in mind with honesty and fairness.

wordCard.voice: Caiaphas. The high priest who said one man should die for the people, which John hears as an unknowing prophecy of Jesus's death.

orig.note: Greek: it is better, it's to our advantage. The King James says expedient.

carryVoice: Your line: for the nation. One sentence, heard two ways: politics and prophecy. Day six hundred twenty-four.
